{{< include ../exercise-header.qmd >}}

::: {#exr-bat-meet-mattress}
Sometimes the dimension of a quantity points to an unexpected way to interpret that quantity. Consider, for example, energy utilization of walking rate *80 Cal per mile*. The dimension of *80 Cal* is [energy]. The dimension of *mile* is [L]. 


1. Which of these is equivalent to [energy]
```{mcq}
#| label: bmm-1-t37s
1. `r bracket("force")` $\div$ `r bracket("length")`
2. `r bracket("force")` $\div$ `r bracket("mass")`
3. `r bracket("force")` $\times$ `r bracket("length")` [correct]
4. `r bracket("mass")` $\times$ `r bracket("time")`
```

2. What is the dimension of the rate *80 Cal per mile*?

```{mcq}
#| label: bmm-2-t37s
1. `r bracket("energy")`
2. `r bracket("force")` [correct]
3. `r bracket("energy")` $\div$ `r bracket("time")` 
4. `r bracket("energy")` $\times$ `r bracket("length")` [hint: notice the *per* in *Cal per mile*.]
```

3. Briefly state your opinion of whether the (correct) answer to 2 is consistent with your intuition of what energy per mile means. 
`r devoirs_text("bmm-3-t37s", )

:::
 <!-- end of exr-bat-meet-mattress -->
